moves.what_it_does: Stop routing new traffic to a worker. Mitigates a fault that software cannot repair (the path to the worker, or load it cannot carry); the cause still needs a human. Refused if no other worker is serving.

payload.expected_effect: New requests will no longer be routed to target‑b through HAProxy; they will be served by target‑a (or other healthy workers). The high‑latency path is temporarily eliminated, restoring acceptable p95 latency for the fleet.
payload.reasoning: target-b is degraded because traffic through HAProxy to it is slow (p95 ~1.6 s) while the worker itself is healthy when reached directly. The fault class is network_path, meaning the software cannot repair the path‑to‑the‑worker issue; a human will need to investigate the HAProxy/tcp‑proxy configuration. Draining target‑b removes the faulty path from the load‑balancer, preventing users from experiencing the high latency. Since target-a is healthy and can serve traffic, the drain is allowed. This move mitigates the user‑visible impact while the path fault is resolved externally.
payload.risk: Drain removes target‑b from rotation; if no other worker were available the system would lose capacity. Here target‑a is healthy, so risk is low. The underlying path fault still needs a human fix; draining only avoids the bad path, it does not repair it.
